options.why: Read the repeating up-and-down pattern as an even spread, but a uniform display has columns of equal height.
Counted only the single tallest column at $8$am and ignored the other two peaks.
Counted only the two tallest peaks at $8$am and $10$am and missed the third peak at $12$pm.

questions.solution_text:
$8$am, $10$am and $12$pm are each taller than the columns on either side of them, so there are three peaks.
Multimodal.

options.why: Saw two stacks of equal height and concluded the whole plot is level, but the other stacks are much shorter.
Counted the two equally tall stacks at $3$ and $4$ as two peaks, but they sit side by side with no dip between them.
Counted every stack that is taller than the one to its left as a peak, which counts the same single rise several times.

questions.solution_text:
The stacks at $3$ and $4$ are equally tall, but they sit side by side with no dip between them, so together they form a single peak.
Every other stack is shorter than its neighbour towards the middle.
Unimodal.

questions.question_text:
The frequency table shows the number of trains arriving each hour, recorded over $38$ hours.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{Trains per hour} & \text{Frequency} \\ \hline 1\text{--}3 & 4 \\ \hline 4\text{--}6 & 12 \\ \hline 7\text{--}9 & 5 \\ \hline 10\text{--}12 & 3 \\ \hline 13\text{--}15 & 10 \\ \hline 16\text{--}18 & 4 \\ \hline \end{array}$
How would you describe the modality of this distribution?

options.why: Treated the data as evenly spread because every class has a non-zero frequency, but the frequencies are not equal.
Reported only the largest frequency of $12$ and ignored the second rise to $10$ at $13\text{--}15$.
Counted $16\text{--}18$ as a third peak, but its frequency of $4$ is lower than the frequency of the class before it.

questions.solution_text:
The frequencies rise to $12$ at $4\text{--}6$, fall to $3$ at $10\text{--}12$, then rise again to $10$ at $13\text{--}15$.
Two peaks separated by a dip.
Bimodal.

questions.question_text:
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.85]\draw[->] (0,0)--(0,4.7);\draw[->] (0,0)--(8.2,0);\draw[thick] plot[smooth,tension=0.6] coordinates {(0.2,0.1)(0.9,1)(1.6,3.3)(2.4,1.4)(3.2,0.8)(4,0.9)(4.8,1.5)(5.6,3)(6.4,1.2)(7.2,0.2)};\node[rotate=90,font=\scriptsize] at (-1.1,1.65) {Number of orders};\node[below,font=\scriptsize] at (3.6,-1.0) {Time of day};\node[font=\small] at (3.6,4.4) {Orders each hour};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
The curve shows the distribution of orders taken at a café through the day. How would you describe the modality of this distribution?

options.why: Assumed a smooth curve spreads the data evenly, but a uniform distribution would be drawn as a flat line.
Counted only the higher of the two high points instead of counting both rises.
Counted the low point between the two high points as a peak as well, but a dip is not a peak.

questions.solution_text:
The curve rises to a high point, dips down, then rises to a second high point before falling away.
Two peaks.
Bimodal.

Each display shows the distribution of a different dataset. Which display shows a unimodal distribution?

options.why: Chose the flat display, which has no peak at all and so is uniform rather than unimodal.
Chose the display with two tall columns separated by a dip, which has two peaks and so is bimodal.

questions.solution_text:
$A$ is flat, so it is uniform. $B$ has two tall columns separated by a dip, so it is bimodal.
$C$ rises to one tallest column and falls away on both sides, so it has exactly one peak.
Display $C$.

options.why: Counted only the tallest column at $5$pm instead of every column taller than both of its neighbours.
Counted only the two tallest peaks at $5$pm and $7$pm and missed the lower peak at $3$pm.
Counted every change of direction in the graph, so the two dips at $4$pm and $6$pm were counted as well as the three peaks.

questions.solution_text:
A column is a peak when it is taller than the columns on either side of it.
$3$pm is taller than $2$pm and $4$pm, $5$pm is taller than $4$pm and $6$pm, and $7$pm is taller than $6$pm and $8$pm.
$3$ peaks.

options.text: Uniform; every value is a mode.
options.why: Read equal frequencies as many modes, but when every value occurs equally often the dataset has no mode.
Read the flat run of equal columns as one wide peak and then quoted a frequency as the mode.
Counted each of the six equal columns as its own peak, but columns of equal height give no peak at all.

questions.solution_text:
All six columns have the same height, so no hour stands out and there is no peak.
Every value occurs equally often, so there is no mode.
Uniform; there is no mode.
